       1      for calling this important hearing.

       8             We appreciate the opportunity to speak with

      13             The Office of the State Comptroller contains

      14      the largest and most knowledgable concentration of

      15      subject-matter experts in the field of municipal

      16      finances in New York State.

      17             Our agency is a premier source for

      18      information on the financial condition of

      19      New York State's local governments.

      20             Our auditors, researchers, and other experts

      22      identifying local government fiscal-stress issues,

      24      discussion of corrective actions by the Executive,

      25      Legislature, local government officials, and





 

                                                                   9
       1      citizens.

       2             In 2012 alone, OSC's division of local

       3      government and school accountability completed more

       4      than 400 audits of individual units of local

       5      government and school districts, including many

       6      financial-condition audits.

       7             Under Comptroller DiNapoli's leadership, this

       8      division has released 56 research-policy reports and

       9      snapshots, each one effectively highlighting an

      10      important topic of interest regarding our local

      13      knowledge.  In fact, our staff has trained over

      17      policy research, Comptroller DiNapoli has charged

      18      our division with the responsibility to assist local

      19      governments in the difficult task of implementing

      20      the tax-cap legislation that was enacted in 2011.

      21             We provide the necessary guidance and online

      22      forum, and statewide training and outreach program,

      23      to assist local officials in meeting their legal

      24      obligations under the statute.

      25             In the first year, our audit staff performed

       1      nearly 800 tax-cap calculations, and helped ensure

       2      that local officials calculated their levy limits

       3      correctly.

       4             OSC staff has developed a multi-year planning

       5      template that has become a standard for many local

       6      officials as they work towards the goal of increased

       7      accountability.

       8             We are also -- we also recently released a

       9      capital-planning template.

      10             And both of those things can be found on our

      11      website.

      12             When Detroit, once one of America's largest

      13      cities and industrial engines, files for bankruptcy

      14      to resolve its fiscal woes, it shines a spotlight on

      15      the financial challenges facing all local

      16      communities around the nation, and, of course, here

      17      in New York.

      18             Many are wondering if Detroit's fiscal

      19      situation and bankruptcy foreshadow what's to come

      20      for other local governments as they continue to

      21      struggle with issues of financial solvency.

      22             Municipal bankruptcies are rare around the

      23      nation, and they have never happened in

      24      New York State, with good reason.

      25             State intervention through conduits, like,





 

                                                                   11
       1      aid to localities or AIM funding, deficit financing,

       2      various types of oversight agencies, and, very

       3      recently, the Governor's restructuring program that

       4      the Senator's just talked about, is the main reason

       5      why no New York State municipality has ever gone

       6      bankrupt.

       7             Our leaders recognize that bankruptcy

       8      proceedings of municipalities in other states have

       9      left fiscal problems unresolved for years, while

      10      making it more difficult for local governments to

      11      deliver essential services.

      12             Comptroller DiNapoli has stated, that, "While

      13      bankruptcy is a legal option for most of

      14      New York State's local governments, it is the least

      15      palatable option and should never occur."

      16             Here in New York, the "Great Recision" and

      17      our slow national recovery have directly affected

      18      several sources of local revenue.

      19             A confluence of factors, including decreasing

      20      tax bases, growing fixed budget costs, losses in

      21      population, and deteriorating industrial sector,

      22      have merged to create chronic budget gaps and

      23      significant fiscal stress in counties, cities,

      24      towns, and villages across New York.

      25             Moreover, even in the post-recession period,





 

                                                                   12
       1      the revenue situation for local governments is

       2      underwhelming at best.

       3             County sales-tax collections for 2012 were

       4      only 3.3 percent over 2011, compared to an annual

       5      average of 5 percent for the decade preceding the

       6      recession.

       7             Losses in mortgage-recording tax revenues are

       8      leveling off, but towns still collected $249 million

       9      less in 2011 than they did in 2005.

      10             The outlook for state and federal aid is also

      11      not promising after a decade of growth below the

      12      rate of inflation.

      13             And, now, growth in local property-tax levies

      14      is limited under the State's property-tax cap.

      15             Evidence that this prolonged fiscal struggle

      16      is having a very real and adverse effect on the

      17      day-to-day operations of local governments is

      18      abundantly clear when we look at some of the metrics

      19      typically employed to examine their financial

      20      situations in August of 2012.

      21             At that time, we found that nearly 300 local

      22      governments had deficits in 2010 or in 2011, and,

      23      more than 100 had inadequate cash on hand to pay

      24      their current bills.

      25             We also know that fund balances are being





 

                                                                   13
       1      depleted at an alarming rate.

       2             In our 2012 annual report, we included a

       3      cautionary note about how unreserved or

       4      non-restricted fund balances, as a percentage of

       5      expenditures, were at their lowest point in a

       6      decade, and had dropped 28 percent since peaking at

       7      9.7 in 2006.

       8             These challenges, and the circumstances that

       9      drive and deplete the fund balances, are likely to

      10      persist for some time.

      11             And I think that we can all agree that

      12      there's no one-size-fit-all approach to effectively

      13      deal with them.

      14             That being said, however, we should not be

      15      deterred from trying to get a better handle on how

      16      these challenges are confronting different

      17      communities across our state.

      18             Before you can attack a problem, you need to

      19      understand what you're facing.

      20             This is why Comptroller DiNapoli commissioned

      21      the development of the fiscal-stress agenda that

      22      includes the fiscal profiles and -- of dozens of

      23      New York State localities and an early warning

      24      system to present a realistic account of local

      25      government finances.





 

                                                                   14
       1             The purpose of this agenda is to help foster

       2      much needed public discussions about fiscal stress,

       3      by clearly defining the issues to be addressed, and

       4      providing accurate and objective data analysis, so

       5      that corrective actions can be taken.

       6             This way, we can reach lasting solution and

       7      avoid steps that may cause needless harm to our

       8      communities.

       9             In other words, we need to continue these

      10      discussions, and take corrective actions as soon as

      11      possible, so that we can avoid the extreme steps now

      12      being considered in Detroit and in certain

      13      jurisdictions across the county.

      14             I will now focus both on the fiscal profiles

      15      and the fiscal-stress monitoring system, also known

      16      as our "early warning system."

      17             In September 2012, the Comptroller released a

      18      report on New York cities, and it was called

      19      "New York Cities:  An Economic and Fiscal Analysis,

      20      1980 through 2010."

      21             This detailed the plight of our once vibrant

      22      cities.

      23             With eroding tax bases, significant losses in

      24      population and industrial sector, neither the

      25      challenges facing cities, nor the impact of their





 

                                                                   15
       1      condition upon the state's own economic and fiscal

       2      well-being, can be ignored.

       3             After Comptroller DiNapoli took on the

       4      critical task of bringing the concerns of our cities

       5      to a public light, he developed the city fiscal

       6      profile as a platform for focusing more attention on

       7      their unique challenges, and how those challenges

       8      influence each city's financial landscape.

       9             The Comptroller has released ten profiles to

      10      date, including Niagara Falls, Salamanca, Rochester,

      11      Yonkers, Syracuse, Gloversville, Utica, Elmira,

      12      Watertown, and Binghamton.

      13             And, we are also poised to release additional

      14      profiles over the next few months.

      15             A fiscal profile constitutes a succinct

      16      factual presentation of the fiscal or budgetary

      17      situation as of a fixed point in time, and is

      18      targeted in tone and depth to both policymakers and

      19      the general tax-paying public.

      20             These profiles have cast a much needed

      21      spotlight on the issues in the state's cities in

      22      particular, but the issues are admittedly, and

      23      unfortunately, much more widespread.

      24             This brings us to our fiscal-stress

      25      monitoring system which is the center piece of the





 

                                                                   16
       1      Comptroller's comprehensive fiscal-stress agenda.

       2             In light of the daunting challenges facing

       3      local governments, our office has developed a

       4      fiscal-stress monitoring system.

       5             The goal of this system is to identify

       6      specific counties, cities, towns, and villages, and,

       7      of course, school districts, that are in significant

       8      stress or approaching stress, and to provide

       9      information on the factors driving that stress to

      10      local officials and taxpayers, so that an effective

      11      plan to reverse the course can be developed.

      12             The system uses 9 fiscal and 14 environmental

      13      indicators.

      14             The financial indicators are calculated using

      15      the financial data already being reported by local

      16      governments in their annual update documents, or

      17      also known as their "AUDs," and school districts

      18      in their annual financial reports, known as their

      19      "ST-3s."

      20             Examples of financial indicators include

      21      changes in year or end fund balance, cash position,

      22      short-term debt, et cetera; while environmental

      23      indicators measure the external influences that are

      24      often beyond the control of the community:

      25      population changes, changes in poverty level,





 

                                                                   17
       1      property-value changes, et cetera.

       2             Although each entity receives an overall

       3      financial-indicator score and an

       4      environmental-indicator score, it's the financial

       5      indicators that are used to categorize each

       6      jurisdiction into one of the three categories of

       7      stress, and that is:  Are there significant fiscal

       8      stress, moderate fiscal stress, or susceptible to

       9      fiscal stress?

      10             An entity not in one of those stress

      11      categories is deemed to have "no designation."

      12             This system ensures that the level of fiscal

      13      stress a municipality is facing -- this system

      14      measures, I should say, the level of fiscal stress a

      15      municipality is facing, and it does not measure the

      16      level of fiscal health.

      17             A municipality's absence from the stress in

      18      one of our three stress categories should not be

      19      viewed as a substantiation of good financial

      20      condition by OSC; rather, it means that the

      21      municipality is simply not displaying the levels of

      22      fiscal stress, as defined by our system, to be

      23      placed in one of those three stress categories.

      24             The effort behind the development of the

      25      system was substantial, and the research and





 

                                                                   18
       1      analytical process that moved it from concept to

       2      completion was an inclusive one.

       3             Our work was informed by a team of internal

      11      100 comments before we finalized the system.

       1      harness the power of data; data that is consistent

      25      what we consider an already rich source of useful

       1      information into local governments' and school

       1      directed our agency to provide extensive -- an
